sk: अथ हैनं भार्गवो वैदर्भिः पप्रच्छ भगवन्कत्येव देवाः प्रजां विधारयन्ते कतर एतत्प्रकाशयन्ते कः पुनरेषां वरिष्ठ इति ||
ro: atha · ha · enaṁ · bhārgavaḥ · vaidarbhiḥ · papraccha · bhagavan · kati · eva · devāḥ · prajāṁ · vidhārayante · kataraḥ · etat · prakāśayante · kaḥ · punaḥ · eṣāṁ · variṣṭhaḥ · iti ||
hi: तब भार्गव वैदर्भि ने (पिप्पलाद से) पूछा — 'भगवन्! कितने देव प्रजा (प्राणी/शरीर) को धारण करते हैं? उनमें से कौन-कौन इसे प्रकाशित (चेतन) करते हैं? और इन सबमें वरिष्ठ (श्रेष्ठ) कौन है?'
en: Then Bhārgava Vaidarbhi asked him: 'Bhagavan! How many gods (devāḥ) support (vidhārayante) the creature (prajā)? Which of them illuminate (prakāśayante) it? And who among them is the greatest (variṣṭha)?'

ws.e: Bhārgava Vaidarbhi — the second questioner; from the Bhṛgu lineage (bhārgava) and the Vidarbha region (vaidarbhi)

ws.h: देवता / शरीर में विद्यमान दिव्य शक्तियाँ
ws.e: gods / divine powers — here referring to the bodily faculties (senses, mind, breath, etc.) that 'shine' within the creature

ws.h: धारण करते हैं / सहारा देते हैं
ws.e: support / sustain — vi + √dhṛ (to hold); causative middle: the gods actively uphold the body-mind complex

ws.h: प्रकाशित करते हैं / चेतन बनाते हैं
ws.e: illuminate / manifest — pra + √kāś (to shine); the gods who make consciousness evident in the creature
greatest / most excellent — superlative of vara (excellent); the one supreme power among all the bodily devas

gr: kati eva devāḥ — 'how many gods exactly?' The word eva (exactly, indeed) shows Bhārgava wants a precise count, not a vague answer. Three-part question: (1) kati devāḥ vidhārayante — how many gods sustain the creature? (2) katare prakāśayante — which ones illuminate it? (3) kaḥ variṣṭhaḥ — who is the greatest? The first asks about number, the second about function, the third about hierarchy. prajā — literally 'offspring/creature', here meaning the embodied being (the body-mind complex supported by various divine faculties). devāḥ — in the Upanishadic context, 'gods' often refers to the sense-faculties and vital powers (indriyas and prāṇas) that operate within the body, each identified with a cosmic deity (Agni with speech, Āditya with sight, etc.).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.1 — The second question shifts from cosmology (Question 1: Prāṇa-Rayi at the macrocosmic level) to physiology — the microcosmic operation of the 'gods' within the individual body. This mirrors the Vedic principle of adhidaiva-adhyātma correspondence: every cosmic deity has a bodily counterpart. The three sub-questions (how many? which illuminate? who is greatest?) set up the famous 'departure test' that follows — the gods will discover their relative importance by seeing what happens when each one leaves the body.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'देव' शब्द यहाँ इन्द्रियों और प्राणों के लिए प्रयुक्त है, क्योंकि ये शरीर में 'दीप्ति' (प्रकाश) उत्पन्न करते हैं। 'विधारयन्ते' — ये शरीर को क्षण-क्षण धारण (sustain) करते हैं। प्रश्न यह है कि इनमें कौन सबसे अधिक अनिवार्य (indispensable) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'devāḥ' here refers to the sense-faculties and vital breaths, because they produce 'luminosity' (dīpti) in the body. 'Vidhārayante' — they sustain the body moment by moment. The real question is: which one is the most indispensable?
advaita.ins: The body is a city with many officials. Each sense-deity lights its own department. But which official holds up the whole city? Remove that one, and the entire administration collapses.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'देव' शब्द से ज्ञात होता है कि ये शक्तियाँ ईश्वर-प्रदत्त हैं — स्वतंत्र नहीं, भगवान् के अंश हैं। शरीर भगवान् का मंदिर है और ये देव उस मंदिर के सेवक हैं। 'वरिष्ठ' — सबसे प्रमुख सेवक भी भगवान् के अधीन है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the word 'devāḥ' indicates these powers are God-given — they are not independent but are aspects of the Lord. The body is the Lord's temple and these gods are servants in that temple. 'Variṣṭha' — even the greatest servant is subordinate to the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Every faculty in your body is a gift from the Divine. Even the 'greatest' among them — Prāṇa — is a servant, not the master. The master is the Lord who delegated these powers.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — यह प्रश्न चेतना के स्तरभेद (hierarchy of consciousness) को उजागर करता है। प्रत्येक 'देव' चेतना का एक विशेष कार्य (function) है — वाक्, चक्षु, मन, प्राण। प्रश्न है: कौन-सा कार्य सबसे मूलभूत है?
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees this question as revealing the hierarchy of consciousness. Each 'deva' is a specific function of consciousness — speech, sight, mind, breath. The question is: which function is the most fundamental?
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness doesn't arrive in the body as one uniform block. It differentiates into seeing, hearing, thinking, breathing. But there's a root-function beneath them all — find that, and you've found the key to the whole system.

dp.q: 🔍 What are the 'gods' (devāḥ) in the body?
dp.a: In Vedic thought, every cosmic deity has a bodily counterpart — this is the adhidaiva-adhyātma (macrocosm-microcosm) correspondence. The 'gods' that sustain the creature are: Prāṇa (vital breath, corresponds to Vāyu/Wind), Vāk (speech, corresponds to Agni/Fire), Cakṣus (sight, corresponds to Āditya/Sun), Śrotra (hearing, corresponds to Diś/Directions), Manas (mind, corresponds to Candra/Moon), plus Ākāśa (space), Āp (water), Pṛthivī (earth), and Tejas (fire). The Upanishad will identify these in the next mantra and then determine which is variṣṭha (greatest) through the famous departure test. The total is traditionally given as five prāṇas + five sense-organs + five action-organs + mind, though this passage focuses on the most prominent ones.

dp.q: 🔍 Why does the question use three sub-parts?
dp.a: Bhārgava's question is methodically structured: (1) kati — 'how many?' establishes the count of divine powers operating in the body. (2) katare prakāśayante — 'which ones illuminate?' distinguishes the active powers (those that produce conscious awareness) from the passive elements (like ākāśa and earth, which support but don't 'shine'). (3) kaḥ variṣṭhaḥ — 'who is greatest?' seeks the hierarchy. This three-part structure mirrors the Sāṅkhya method of analysis: enumerate, classify, rank. The question is not merely philosophical — it has practical yogic implications. If you know which faculty is supreme, you know where to concentrate your meditation. The answer (Prāṇa) is why prāṇāyāma (breath-control) became the central practice in yoga.

sk: तस्मै स होवाचाकाशो ह वा एष देवो वायुरग्निरापः पृथिवी वाङ्मनश्चक्षुः श्रोत्रं च ते प्रकाश्याभिवदन्ति वयमेतद्बाणमवष्टभ्य विधारयामः ||
ro: tasmai · saḥ · ha · uvāca · ākāśaḥ · ha · vā · eṣaḥ · devaḥ · vāyuḥ · agniḥ · āpaḥ · pṛthivī · vāk · manaḥ · cakṣuḥ · śrotraṁ · ca · te · prakāśya · abhivadanti · vayam · etat · bāṇam · avaṣṭabhya · vidhārayāmaḥ ||
hi: उनसे उन्होंने (पिप्पलाद ने) कहा — 'आकाश, वायु, अग्नि, जल, पृथ्वी — ये (पाँच महाभूत) और वाक् (वाणी), मन, चक्षु (दृष्टि), श्रोत्र (श्रवण) — ये देव हैं। वे (अपनी महिमा) प्रकट करते हुए कहते हैं — हम ही इस शरीररूपी बाण (स्तम्भ/शरीर) को अवष्टभ्य (थामकर/सहारा देकर) धारण करते हैं।'
en: To him he (Pippalāda) said: 'Space (ākāśa), air (vāyu), fire (agni), water (āpaḥ), earth (pṛthivī) — and speech (vāk), mind (manas), sight (cakṣuḥ), and hearing (śrotra) — these are the gods. Having manifested (their glory), they declare: "We, supporting this body (bāṇa), sustain it."'

ws.e: space / ether — the first and subtlest of the five great elements (pañca-mahābhūta); provides the medium in which all other elements operate
speech — the faculty of vocal expression; its presiding deity is Agni (Fire)
mind — the internal organ of thought and will; its presiding deity is Candra (Moon)

ws.h: शरीर / स्तम्भ (बाण = सरकण्डा / शरीर का रूपक)
ws.e: body (literally 'reed-shaft' or 'arrow') — the body is compared to a hollow shaft (bāṇa/veṇu) supported by the gods; some read this as 'pillar' (sthāṇu) — a structure held up by multiple supports
having supported / propped up — ava + √stambh (to support, prop); the gods collectively hold up the body like pillars holding a roof

gr: Nine devas are enumerated: five elements (ākāśa, vāyu, agni, āpaḥ, pṛthivī) + four faculties (vāk, manas, cakṣuḥ, śrotra). This is not the standard list of five jñānendriyas; it mixes elements and faculties to show the adhidaiva-adhyātma unity. bāṇam — a striking metaphor: the body is a bāṇa (reed-shaft, arrow, or hollow stalk). Just as a reed stands only because its fibres support it from within, the body stands only because multiple divine powers hold it together from inside. abhivadanti — 'they declare/boast': each god claims credit for sustaining the body. This sets up the contest in the next mantra — all claim supremacy, but only one will prove it. prakāśya — absolutive of pra-√kāś: 'having illuminated / manifested their glory'. The gods first demonstrate their power and then make their claim.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.2 — The enumeration of nine devas (5 elements + 4 faculties) corresponds roughly to the Sāṅkhya taxonomy but is not identical — Sāṅkhya has 5 tanmātras + 5 jñānendriyas + 5 karmendriyas + manas. The Upanishadic list is deliberately selective, combining cosmic elements with their conscious counterparts. The metaphor of the body as bāṇa (reed) appears only here and is unique to the Prashna. The departure-test motif that follows (mantras 3-4) parallels the famous Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.1 and Chāndogya 5.1 passages where prāṇa proves its supremacy.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — नौ देवताओं का उल्लेख शरीर के पंचभौतिक (five-elemental) और चेतन (conscious) दोनों पक्षों को दिखाता है। 'बाण' — शरीर एक खोखले नलकी (reed) की तरह है, जिसे ये नौ शक्तियाँ भीतर से थामती हैं। प्रत्येक का दावा है कि 'मैं श्रेष्ठ हूँ' — यह अहंकार का प्रतीक है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the nine deities reveal both the elemental (pañca-bhautika) and conscious aspects of the body. 'Bāṇa' — the body is like a hollow reed held up from within by these nine powers. Each one claims 'I am the greatest' — this is symbolic of the ego's tendency to claim credit.
advaita.ins: Nine gods, nine pillars, one hollow reed. Each pillar thinks it alone holds up the roof. The reed doesn't care about their debate — it stands only because of the one power that can't be argued away.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — ये नौ देव ईश्वर के विभूतियाँ (vibhūtis, divine manifestations) हैं — आकाश से लेकर श्रोत्र तक। शरीर भगवान् का क्षेत्र (field) है और ये देव उस क्षेत्र के अधिष्ठातृ (presiding officers) हैं। उनका दावा 'हम धारण करते हैं' — किन्तु वस्तुतः ईश्वर ही धारण करते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says these nine gods are vibhūtis (divine manifestations) of the Lord — from space down to hearing. The body is the Lord's kṣetra (field) and these gods are its presiding officers. They claim 'we sustain it' — but in reality the Lord alone sustains.
vishisht.ins: The officers think they run the city. But every one of them is appointed by a king they can't see. Remove the king's authority, and the officers are just jobless mortals.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — पाँच तत्त्व (elements) शरीर का भौतिक आधार हैं, जबकि चार इन्द्रियाँ (वाक्, मन, चक्षु, श्रोत्र) चेतना के द्वार (gateways of consciousness) हैं। शरीर को 'बाण' कहना — यह शरीर की क्षणभंगुरता (fragility) को दर्शाता है: एक तिनके की तरह, जो किसी भी क्षण टूट सकता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the five elements form the material basis of the body, while the four faculties (speech, mind, sight, hearing) are gateways of consciousness. Calling the body 'bāṇa' (reed) indicates its fragility — like a stalk that can snap at any moment.
aurobindo.ins: Your body is a reed standing in a field. Wind, fire, water, earth — these hold it from outside. Mind, speech, sight, hearing — these light it from inside. But what makes the reed alive? That's the question the gods are about to answer.

dp.q: 🔍 Why are five elements and four faculties listed together?
dp.a: The Upanishad deliberately mixes cosmic elements (ākāśa, vāyu, agni, āpaḥ, pṛthivī) with cognitive faculties (vāk, manas, cakṣuḥ, śrotra) to illustrate the adhidaiva-adhyātma principle: every cosmic power has a bodily counterpart. Space manifests in the body as the cavities (ears, nostrils, throat). Air manifests as Prāṇa. Fire manifests as body-heat and digestion. Water manifests as blood, lymph, and fluids. Earth manifests as bone, flesh, and solid tissue. The four faculties represent the conscious aspect: without speech, mind, sight, and hearing, the body would be alive but not aware. Together, the nine cover both existence (the elements keep the body materially intact) and experience (the faculties make consciousness possible). The question 'who is greatest?' thus asks: is existence more fundamental than experience, or vice versa?

dp.q: 🔍 What is the 'bāṇa' (body-as-reed) metaphor?
dp.a: The word bāṇa literally means 'reed-shaft' or 'arrow'. The body is compared to a hollow reed (veṇu or śara) — a structure that appears solid but is actually empty inside, sustained entirely by the forces that pass through it. This is a profound metaphor: (1) Fragility: a reed breaks easily. The body, for all its apparent strength, collapses the moment its sustaining powers withdraw. (2) Hollowness: the body has no self-sustaining substance; it depends entirely on the 'gods' (elements and faculties) that fill and support it. (3) Musicality: a reed (veṇu) becomes a flute when breath passes through it. Similarly, the body becomes a living, conscious being only when Prāṇa (life-breath) passes through it. Without Prāṇa, the body is a silent, dead reed. This sets up the answer to 'who is variṣṭha?' — it is the breath that makes the reed sing.

sk: तान्वरिष्ठः प्राण उवाच मा मोहमापद्यथ अहमेवैतत्पञ्चधात्मानं प्रविभज्यैतद्बाणमवष्टभ्य विधारयामीति ते ऽश्रद्दधाना बभूवुः ||
ro: tān · variṣṭhaḥ · prāṇaḥ · uvāca · mā · moham · āpadyatha · aham · eva · etat · pañcadhā · ātmānaṁ · pravibhajya · etat · bāṇam · avaṣṭabhya · vidhārayāmi · iti · te · aśraddadhānāḥ · babhūvuḥ ||
hi: उनसे (उन देवों से) वरिष्ठ प्राण ने कहा — 'मोह में मत पड़ो! मैं ही अपने आपको पाँच भागों में विभक्त करके इस शरीररूपी बाण (स्तम्भ) को अवष्टभ्य (थामकर) धारण करता हूँ।' किन्तु वे (अन्य देव) अश्रद्धालु (विश्वास न करने वाले) हो गए।
en: To them the greatest (variṣṭha), Prāṇa, said: 'Do not fall into delusion! I alone, having divided myself fivefold (pañcadhā), support and sustain this body (bāṇa).' But they became disbelieving (aśraddadhānāḥ).

ws.e: the greatest, Prāṇa — the vital breath declares itself the supreme deity; variṣṭha is the superlative of vara (excellent)
delusion / confusion — from √muh (to be bewildered); Prāṇa warns the other gods against the delusion of self-importance

ws.h: पाँच प्रकार से / पाँच भागों में
ws.e: fivefold — the five forms of Prāṇa: prāṇa (outward breath), apāna (downward breath), vyāna (diffused breath), udāna (upward breath), samāna (equalising breath)
having divided — pra + vi + √bhaj (to divide); absolutive: Prāṇa first divides itself, then supports the body through its five forms
disbelieving / without faith — a (not) + śrad + √dhā (to place faith); the other gods refuse to accept Prāṇa's claim

gr: variṣṭhaḥ prāṇaḥ uvāca — the narrator already calls Prāṇa 'the greatest' (variṣṭha) before the proof is given — a literary technique that previews the outcome. pañcadhā ātmānaṁ pravibhajya — 'having divided myself fivefold': the five prāṇas (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna) are not five separate entities but one Prāṇa operating in five modes. This is significant — it means the 'support' of the body is not distributed among independent powers but is a single unified force manifesting in five directions. aśraddadhānāḥ — the gods 'became disbelieving'. This incredulity is dramatically necessary: it sets up the departure-test in the next mantra. If they had believed, there would be no demonstration.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.3 — The fivefold division of Prāṇa (pañca-prāṇa) is a foundational concept in Vedānta, Yoga, and Āyurveda. The five are: (1) prāṇa — governs inhalation and upward-moving breath, seated in the chest; (2) apāna — governs exhalation and downward-moving functions (excretion, reproduction), seated below the navel; (3) samāna — governs digestion and assimilation, seated in the abdomen; (4) udāna — governs upward movement at death and in speech, seated in the throat; (5) vyāna — pervades the entire body, governs circulation. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.3), Chāndogya (5.1), and Kauṣītaki (2.14) all contain parallel accounts of Prāṇa's supremacy.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्राण का 'पञ्चधा विभजन' यह दर्शाता है कि एक ही चैतन्य-शक्ति (conscious force) पाँच कार्यों में प्रकट होती है। जैसे एक राजा पाँच मंत्रियों के रूप में शासन करता है, वैसे ही प्राण पाँच रूपों में शरीर को चलाता है। अन्य देवों का अविश्वास — अज्ञान (avidyā) का लक्षण है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Prāṇa's 'fivefold division' shows that one conscious force manifests in five functions. Just as a king governs through five ministers, Prāṇa operates the body through five forms. The other gods' disbelief is a sign of avidyā (ignorance).
advaita.ins: One breath, five jobs. The mistake of the other gods is thinking each function is a separate power. It's like five rivers arguing about which one is the 'real' water — they're all the same ocean, branching.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण जो कहता है 'मैं ही धारण करता हूँ' — यह ईश्वर की शक्ति के माध्यम से है। प्राण स्वयं ईश्वर का सबसे प्रमुख उपकरण (instrument) है। अन्य देवों का अविश्वास — यह जीव का स्वतंत्रता-भ्रम (illusion of independence) है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Prāṇa's claim 'I alone sustain' is through the Lord's power. Prāṇa itself is the Lord's foremost instrument. The other gods' disbelief represents the jīva's illusion of independence.
vishisht.ins: Prāṇa doesn't speak for itself alone. It speaks as the Lord's chief agent. When the prime minister says 'I govern this country', he means 'through the authority vested in me by the sovereign.'

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण का पाँच रूपों में विभाजन चेतना के उतरने (descent of consciousness) की प्रक्रिया को दर्शाता है — एक मूल शक्ति विभिन्न स्तरों पर भिन्न-भिन्न कार्य करती है। अन्य इन्द्रियों का अविश्वास — यह अहंकार का स्वाभाविक प्रतिरोध (resistance) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees Prāṇa's fivefold division as illustrating the descent of consciousness — one root-force performing different functions at different levels. The other faculties' disbelief is the natural resistance of the ego.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness descends into the body like light through a prism — one beam, five colours. Each colour thinks it's independent. The prism-test is about to prove them wrong.

dp.q: 🔍 What are the five forms of Prāṇa?
dp.a: The pañca-prāṇa (five vital breaths) are: (1) Prāṇa (capital-P) — the forward/upward-moving breath, governing inhalation, swallowing, and sensory intake; seated in the chest and head; associated with the face (mukha-prāṇa). (2) Apāna — the downward-moving breath, governing excretion, urination, reproduction, and exhalation's final phase; seated below the navel. (3) Samāna — the 'equalising' breath, governing digestion and assimilation; it distributes the essence of food throughout the body; seated in the abdomen near the navel-fire (jāṭharāgni). (4) Udāna — the upward-moving breath, governing speech, effort, and the departure of the soul at death; seated in the throat. (5) Vyāna — the 'pervading' breath, governing circulation of blood and nutrients throughout the entire body; it has no single seat but pervades all limbs. Together, these five are not separate substances but five modes of one Prāṇa — like five currents in one river.

dp.q: 🔍 Why do the other gods disbelieve Prāṇa?
dp.a: The disbelief (aśraddhā) of the other gods is both a narrative device and a philosophical point. Narratively, their disbelief forces Prāṇa to demonstrate its supremacy through the departure-test (mantra 4) — making the proof dramatic and irrefutable. Philosophically, each faculty genuinely experiences itself as essential: speech 'knows' that without it the body cannot communicate, sight 'knows' that without it the body is blind, and so on. Each deity's experience of its own importance is real but partial. The error is mistaking a partial truth for the whole truth — the classic Vedāntic definition of avidyā (ignorance). This mirrors the human condition: each organ of knowledge thinks it is the most important, just as each individual ego thinks it is the centre of the universe. Only the departure of Prāṇa reveals the dependency that all other faculties have on it.

sk: स उद्क्रामन्निव तान्सर्वानुद्क्रामयते स प्रतिष्ठमानस्तान्सर्वान्प्रतिष्ठापयति तद्यथा मक्षिका मधुकरराजानमुद्क्रामन्तं सर्वा एवोद्क्रामन्ति तस्मिंश्च प्रतिष्ठमाने सर्वा एव प्रतितिष्ठन्ते एवं वाङ्मनश्चक्षुः श्रोत्रं च ते प्रीताः प्राणं स्तुन्वन्ति ||
ro: saḥ · utkrāmann · iva · tān · sarvān · utkrāmayate · saḥ · pratiṣṭhamānaḥ · tān · sarvān · pratiṣṭhāpayati · tat · yathā · makṣikāḥ · madhukara-rājānam · utkrāmantaṁ · sarvāḥ · eva · utkrāmanti · tasmin · ca · pratiṣṭhamāne · sarvāḥ · eva · pratitiṣṭhante · evaṁ · vāk · manaḥ · cakṣuḥ · śrotraṁ · ca · te · prītāḥ · prāṇaṁ · stunvanti ||
hi: वह (प्राण) उत्क्रमण (शरीर से निकलने) करते हुए-से हुआ तो उन सबको (अन्य सभी देवों को) भी उत्क्रमण करा दिया (उखाड़ ले गया)। और जब वह प्रतिष्ठित हुआ (लौटकर ठहरा), तो उन सबको भी प्रतिष्ठित कर दिया। जैसे मधुमक्खियाँ (मक्षिकाः) — जब मधुकर-राजा (रानी मक्खी) उड़ जाती है तो सब मक्खियाँ उड़ जाती हैं, और जब वह बैठ जाती है तो सब बैठ जाती हैं — वैसे ही वाक्, मन, चक्षु, श्रोत्र — ये सब प्रसन्न होकर प्राण की स्तुति करने लगे।
en: When he (Prāṇa) made as if to depart, he drew all of them out (utkrāmayate). When he settled back (pratiṣṭhamāna), he re-established them all. Just as when the queen-bee (madhukara-rājāna) departs, all the bees depart, and when she settles, all settle — so speech, mind, sight, and hearing, delighted, praised Prāṇa.

ws.h: ऊपर उठकर जाने वाला / निकलने वाला
ws.e: departing / rising up to leave — ut + √kram (to step); when Prāṇa 'steps up' to leave, all other faculties are pulled out with it

ws.h: पुनः स्थापित होने वाला / ठहरने वाला
ws.e: settling back / becoming established — prati + √sthā (to stand); when Prāṇa returns to its seat, all faculties resume their functions
bees — the simile compares the sense-faculties to bees that follow their queen (Prāṇa) wherever it goes
king of the bees / queen-bee — madhukara (honey-maker, bee) + rājan (king/ruler); the ancient text says 'king' but refers to the leader of the hive

ws.h: स्तुति करते हैं / प्रशंसा करते हैं
ws.e: they praise — from √stu (to praise); the other gods, now convinced, compose a hymn of praise to Prāṇa

gr: utkrāmann iva — 'as if departing': the iva (as if) is significant. Prāṇa did not fully depart — it merely began to leave, and that was enough to pull all other faculties with it. This is the 'departure test' found in parallel at Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.1.7-14 and Chāndogya 5.1.6-15. madhukara-rājānam — the bee-queen simile is memorable and precise: bees don't decide individually to follow the queen; they are compelled by her pheromones. Similarly, the sense-faculties don't choose to follow Prāṇa — they are constitutively dependent on it. Without Prāṇa, they literally cannot function. prītāḥ prāṇaṁ stunvanti — 'delighted, they praised Prāṇa': the vindication of Prāṇa leads directly to the hymn of praise that occupies mantras 5-12. The word prītāḥ (delighted) suggests that recognition of truth brings joy, not humiliation.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.4 — This is the famous 'departure test' (utkrānti-parīkṣā) motif. Parallel versions: (1) Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.1.7-14 — speech, sight, hearing, and mind each depart for a year; the body survives without each. But when Prāṇa begins to depart, all are uprooted like a horse pulling up pegs. (2) Chāndogya 5.1.6-15 — nearly identical, with the added detail that the other gods 'tremble like a great horse about to pull up its tethering pegs'. (3) Kauṣītaki 2.14 — Prāṇa is identified with Brahman on the basis of this test. The Prashna version is more compact and uses the unique bee-queen simile instead of the horse-peg metaphor.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्राण का उत्क्रमण-परीक्षण (departure-test) यह सिद्ध करता है कि प्राण ही एकमात्र स्वतंत्र शक्ति है; अन्य सब परतंत्र (dependent) हैं। यह अध्यात्म में 'नेति-नेति' विधि का पूर्वरूप है — जब तक आप सब कुछ हटा न दें, आप नहीं जान सकते कि क्या अनिवार्य है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the departure-test proves that Prāṇa alone is the independent (svatantra) power; all others are dependent (paratantra). This prefigures the 'neti-neti' method in metaphysics — until you remove everything, you cannot know what is truly indispensable.
advaita.ins: The test is simple but devastating: pull one plug and see what goes dark. Every other plug can be pulled without total collapse. Only Prāṇa's departure kills the entire system. That's how you find what's fundamental — not by argument, but by subtraction.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — मधुमक्खी-रानी की उपमा यह दिखाती है कि प्राण ईश्वर का मुख्य प्रतिनिधि है — जैसे रानी के बिना छत्ता बिखर जाता है, वैसे प्राण के बिना शरीर बिखर जाता है। किन्तु रानी भी ईश्वर के अधीन है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the bee-queen simile shows that Prāṇa is the Lord's chief representative — as the hive disintegrates without the queen, so the body disintegrates without Prāṇa. But even the queen is subordinate to the Lord.
vishisht.ins: The queen-bee runs the hive, but she didn't build it. She's the administrator, not the architect. Prāṇa runs the body, but the Lord designed the system.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण का उत्क्रमण-परीक्षण यह दर्शाता है कि शरीर में एक 'प्राणमय चेतना' (vital consciousness) है जो सब इन्द्रियों से अधिक मूलभूत है। यह योगिक अनुभव की पुष्टि है — प्राणायाम में जब प्राण नियंत्रित होता है, तो मन और इन्द्रियाँ स्वतः शान्त हो जाती हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the departure-test reveals a 'vital consciousness' (prāṇamaya caitanya) in the body that is more fundamental than any sense-faculty. This confirms yogic experience — in prāṇāyāma, when Prāṇa is controlled, mind and senses automatically become quiet.
aurobindo.ins: Control the breath and the mind follows. This is not a technique discovered by accident — it works because Prāṇa is the root, and mind and senses are branches. Shake the root, and every branch trembles.

dp.q: 🔍 The departure-test in Vedic literature
dp.a: The departure test (utkrānti-parīkṣā) appears in three major Upanishads: (1) Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.1.7-14: Speech departs for a year — the body continues, mute but alive. Sight departs — the body continues, blind but alive. Hearing, mind, and seed each depart in turn — the body survives. But when Prāṇa begins to leave, it uproots all the others 'as a great horse might pull up the pegs to which it is tethered.' The faculties then acknowledge: 'You are the greatest; do not depart!' (2) Chāndogya 5.1.6-15: Nearly identical, adding that the gods 'tremble' when Prāṇa stirs. The conclusion: 'They do not call them speech-deities or sight-deities; they call them prāṇa-deities, for Prāṇa alone is all of these.' (3) Prashna 2.4 (this mantra): The most compact version. Instead of year-long departures, Prāṇa merely 'makes as if to leave' (utkrāmann iva) — a single moment suffices. The unique bee-queen simile replaces the horse-peg metaphor. All three versions reach the same conclusion: Prāṇa is variṣṭha — the supreme vital force on which all other faculties depend.

dp.q: 🔍 Why the bee-queen simile?
dp.a: The bee-queen simile (madhukara-rājan) is unique to the Prashna Upanishad and captures several features of the Prāṇa-faculty relationship: (1) Automatic dependence: bees don't decide to follow the queen — they are compelled by her presence. Similarly, the faculties don't choose to depend on Prāṇa; their dependence is structural, not voluntary. (2) Collective collapse: when the queen leaves, the entire hive disperses — not gradually, but all at once. Similarly, when Prāṇa departs, all faculties cease simultaneously (death). (3) Invisible leadership: in a hive, the queen is hidden deep inside. She doesn't 'appear' to lead. Similarly, Prāṇa operates below the level of conscious awareness — you don't 'see' it the way you see sight or 'hear' it the way you hear hearing. Its supremacy is invisible but absolute. The metaphor also carries an evolutionary resonance: the hive is a superorganism, and the body is a superorganism of faculties. The queen-bee is the organising principle that turns a swarm of independent insects into a unified whole — just as Prāṇa turns a collection of sense-organs into a living being.

sk: एषो ऽग्निस्तपत्येष सूर्य एष पर्जन्यो मघवानेष वायुः एष पृथिवी रयिर्देवः सदसच्चामृतं च यत् ||
ro: eṣaḥ · agniḥ · tapati · eṣaḥ · sūryaḥ · eṣaḥ · parjanyaḥ · maghavān · eṣaḥ · vāyuḥ · eṣaḥ · pṛthivī · rayiḥ · devaḥ · sat · asat · ca · amṛtaṁ · ca · yat ||
hi: यह (प्राण) ही अग्नि है जो तपता है, यह सूर्य है, यह पर्जन्य (वर्षा का देवता) है, यह मघवान् (इन्द्र) है, यह वायु है, यह पृथ्वी है, यह रयि (पदार्थ/द्रव्य) है, यह देव है। जो सत् (व्यक्त) है, जो असत् (अव्यक्त) है, और जो अमृत (अविनाशी) है — वह सब प्राण ही है।
en: This (Prāṇa) is the fire that burns, this is the sun, this is the rain-god (Parjanya), this is Indra (Maghavān), this is the wind, this is the earth, this is matter (rayi), this is the god. That which is existent (sat) and non-existent (asat), and that which is immortal (amṛta) — all this is Prāṇa.

ws.e: Parjanya — the rain-god; Vedic deity of the rain-cloud; Prāṇa is identified with the cosmic power that brings rain and fertility
Maghavān — an epithet of Indra meaning 'the bountiful one'; Prāṇa is identified with the king of the gods
matter / wealth / substance — rayi here recalls Question 1 where Rayi (matter) was paired with Prāṇa (energy); now Prāṇa subsumes even its own counterpart
the existent / manifest — what can be perceived and known

ws.h: अव्यक्त / जो दृष्टि में न आए
ws.e: the non-existent / unmanifest — what lies beyond perception; the potential, the latent
the immortal — a (not) + mṛta (dead); that which transcends both sat and asat

gr: eṣaḥ...eṣaḥ...eṣaḥ — the six-fold repetition of 'this is' creates a litany of identification: Prāṇa = fire = sun = rain = Indra = wind = earth. This is the Upanishadic method of adhyāropa (superimposition): identifying the microcosmic with the macrocosmic. sat-asat-amṛta — a three-fold ontological classification: (1) sat — the manifest, existent world; (2) asat — the unmanifest, potential, pre-creation state; (3) amṛta — the immortal, which transcends both existence and non-existence. By identifying Prāṇa with all three, the hymn elevates Prāṇa from a bodily function to a cosmic principle. rayiḥ devaḥ — 'matter and the divine': in Question 1, Prāṇa and Rayi were a duality (energy and matter); here Prāṇa absorbs Rayi into itself, resolving the duality into unity.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.5 — This is the first verse of the hymn of praise (stuti) sung by the faculties to Prāṇa (mantras 5-12). The hymn progressively elevates Prāṇa from a bodily vital force to a cosmic principle encompassing all deities, all elements, and finally all of reality (sat-asat-amṛta). Compare Rig Veda 10.90 (Puruṣa Sūkta) where the Cosmic Person is similarly identified with everything. The sat-asat-amṛta triad echoes the Nāsadīya Sūkta (RV 10.129) and anticipates the Gītā's sat-asat-tatpara classification.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्राण को अग्नि, सूर्य आदि से अभिन्न बताना — यह सगुण ब्रह्म (Brahman with attributes) की उपासना है। सत्-असत्-अमृत — ये तीनों प्राण में समाहित हैं, अर्थात् प्राण यहाँ ब्रह्म का प्रतीक (symbol) बन गया है।
advaita.en: Shankara says identifying Prāṇa with fire, sun, etc. is meditation on saguṇa Brahman (Brahman with attributes). Sat-asat-amṛta — all three are contained in Prāṇa, meaning Prāṇa here becomes a symbol of Brahman itself.
advaita.ins: The hymn lifts Prāṇa from the chest cavity to the cosmos. When the Upanishad says 'Prāṇa is fire, sun, rain' — it's not biology anymore. It's pointing at the one Reality wearing every mask.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण का सर्वव्यापी स्वरूप ईश्वर की सर्वव्यापकता को दर्शाता है। प्राण स्वयं ब्रह्म नहीं है, किन्तु ब्रह्म की सबसे निकटवर्ती शक्ति (proximate power) है। 'सत्-असत्-अमृत' — ये भगवान् के तीन विभाग हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Prāṇa's all-pervading nature reflects the all-pervasiveness of the Lord. Prāṇa is not Brahman itself but is Brahman's most proximate power. 'Sat-asat-amṛta' — these are three departments of the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Prāṇa is the thread that runs through every bead on the necklace — fire, sun, rain, earth. But the thread is not the jeweller. It's the Lord's instrument, not the Lord.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण यहाँ 'ब्रह्माण्डीय प्राण' (cosmic Prāṇa) बन गया है — अग्नि, सूर्य, वर्षा, वायु — ये सब उसी एक शक्ति के भिन्न-भिन्न आविर्भाव (manifestations) हैं। सत्-असत् — व्यक्त और अव्यक्त; अमृत — जो दोनों से परे है — यही सुप्रामेंटल तत्त्व (supramental reality) है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says Prāṇa here becomes 'cosmic Prāṇa' — fire, sun, rain, wind are all manifestations of one force. Sat-asat — the manifest and the unmanifest; amṛta — that which is beyond both — this is the supramental reality.
aurobindo.ins: One force, wearing the mask of fire when it burns, the mask of sun when it shines, the mask of rain when it falls. Strip away the masks, and you find — not nothing, but the immortal (amṛta) that was there before the masks were put on.

dp.q: 🔍 How does Prāṇa become cosmic?
dp.a: The hymn of praise (mantras 5-12) performs a remarkable expansion: Prāṇa begins as a bodily vital force (the breath that sustains the body) and is progressively identified with every cosmic power. The logic follows the Vedic bandhutā (correspondence) principle: Breath ↔ Wind: the air inside the body (prāṇa) is the same substance as the wind outside (vāyu). Body-heat ↔ Fire/Sun: the digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) in the body is a miniature sun. Bodily fluids ↔ Rain: water in the body corresponds to Parjanya (rain). Bodily solids ↔ Earth: bone and flesh correspond to pṛthivī. By the end of the litany, Prāṇa has absorbed sat (all that exists), asat (all that is latent/potential), and amṛta (the deathless ground of reality). This is the Upanishadic ascent from physiology to metaphysics — the same move that turns 'the breath in your nostrils' into 'the ground of all being'.

dp.q: 🔍 What do sat, asat, and amṛta mean here?
dp.a: This triad appears across Vedic literature with consistent meaning: Sat (सत्) — literally 'being', 'the existent'. In this context: the manifest world, everything that can be perceived, named, and known. The universe as we experience it. Asat (असत्) — literally 'non-being', 'the non-existent'. Not mere nothingness, but the unmanifest — the potential, the seed-state from which the manifest world emerges. The Nāsadīya Sūkta (RV 10.129) asks: 'There was neither sat nor asat in the beginning.' Amṛta (अमृत) — literally 'not-dead', 'the immortal'. That which transcends both existence and non-existence — the eternal ground. In Advaita, this is nirguṇa Brahman. By saying Prāṇa encompasses all three, the hymn asserts that Prāṇa is not just a force within reality — it is reality in all its dimensions: manifest, unmanifest, and eternal.

sk: अरा इव रथनाभौ प्राणे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितम् ऋचो यजूंषि सामानि यज्ञः क्षत्रं ब्रह्म च ||
ro: arāḥ · iva · ratha-nābhau · prāṇe · sarvaṁ · pratiṣṭhitam · ṛcaḥ · yajūṁṣi · sāmāni · yajñaḥ · kṣatraṁ · brahma · ca ||
hi: जैसे रथ के नाभि (hub) में सब अरे (spokes) जुड़े होते हैं, वैसे ही प्राण में सब कुछ प्रतिष्ठित है — ऋचाएँ (ऋग्वेद), यजुः (यजुर्वेद), सामगान (सामवेद), यज्ञ, क्षत्र (क्षत्रिय-शक्ति) और ब्रह्म (ब्राह्मण-तेज/ब्रह्मविद्या) — सब प्राण में स्थित हैं।
en: As spokes (arāḥ) are fixed in the hub (nābhi) of a wheel, so in Prāṇa everything is established — the Ṛk verses, the Yajus formulae, the Sāman chants, sacrifice (yajña), the warrior-power (kṣatra), and the priestly-wisdom (brahma).

ws.e: spokes — the radial bars connecting the rim to the hub of a wheel; each spoke depends on the hub for its position and function

ws.h: रथ के पहिये की नाभि (hub) में
ws.e: in the hub of a chariot-wheel — ratha (chariot) + nābhi (navel/hub); locative case; the hub is the centre on which everything turns
Ṛk verses — the hymns of the Ṛg Veda; representing revealed knowledge
Yajus formulae — the sacrificial formulas of the Yajur Veda; representing ritual action
warrior-power / temporal authority — kṣatra represents political and military power; contrasted with brahma (spiritual authority)
priestly-wisdom / sacred knowledge — here brahma (short 'a') means the Veda or the priestly class, not Brahman (the Absolute)

gr: arāḥ iva ratha-nābhau — the wheel-hub simile is one of the most celebrated in Upanishadic literature (cf. Muṇḍaka 2.2.6, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.5.15). The hub is the centre that holds all spokes in place; remove the hub and the wheel collapses. Similarly, Prāṇa is the centre on which all of reality (Vedas, sacrifice, social order) depends. ṛcaḥ yajūṁṣi sāmāni — the three Vedas represent the totality of sacred knowledge. yajñaḥ — sacrifice, the central institution of Vedic religion. kṣatraṁ brahma ca — temporal power and spiritual authority — the two pillars of Vedic society. By saying all these depend on Prāṇa, the hymn asserts that without the vital force, neither knowledge, nor ritual, nor society can exist.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.6 — The wheel-hub simile (ratha-nābhi) recurs across the Upanishads: Muṇḍaka 2.2.6 ('In him the channels are fixed like spokes in a hub'), Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.5.15 ('In this Self all beings are fixed like spokes in a hub'), Kaṭha 2.3.1 (the inverted aśvattha with roots above). The Prashna version is distinctive in what it lists as 'spokes': not just elements or beings, but the three Vedas + sacrifice + the two social powers (kṣatra and brahma). This turns Prāṇa into the foundation of both cosmic and social order.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — रथ-नाभि का दृष्टान्त यह दिखाता है कि प्राण (= ब्रह्म) सब ज्ञान, कर्म, और व्यवस्था का आधार है। बिना प्राण के वेद, यज्ञ, और समाज — सब अरों की तरह बिखर जाते हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says the wheel-hub analogy shows that Prāṇa (= Brahman) is the foundation of all knowledge, action, and social order. Without Prāṇa, the Vedas, sacrifice, and society scatter like spokes without a hub.
advaita.ins: Pull out the hub and the wheel is just a pile of sticks. Pull out Prāṇa and the Vedas are just syllables, the sacrifice is just fire, and society is just a crowd. The hub doesn't look impressive — but it's the one piece that makes everything else a wheel.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण भगवान् के धर्म-चक्र (cosmic wheel) की नाभि है। ऋक्, यजुः, साम — ये भगवान् के तीन प्रकार के वचन हैं। यज्ञ — उनकी सेवा। क्षत्र और ब्रह्म — उनकी दो भुजाएँ (शासन और ज्ञान)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Prāṇa is the hub of the Lord's dharma-wheel (cosmic wheel). The Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman are three modes of the Lord's speech. Sacrifice is His service. Kṣatra and brahma are His two arms (governance and knowledge).
vishisht.ins: God's wheel has many spokes — knowledge, ritual, power, wisdom. But it turns on one axle: the vital force He breathed into creation.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण को नाभि कहना — यह चेतना के केन्द्रीकरण (centralisation of consciousness) का प्रतीक है। ज्ञान (ऋक्), कर्म (यजुः), भाव (साम) — ये तीनों एक केन्द्र (प्राण/चेतना) से निकलते हैं और वहीं लौटते हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says calling Prāṇa the hub symbolises the centralisation of consciousness. Knowledge (Ṛk), action (Yajus), feeling (Sāman) — all three emerge from and return to one centre (Prāṇa/consciousness).
aurobindo.ins: Knowledge, action, and devotion aren't three separate disciplines. They're three spokes of one wheel, and the wheel turns on a single point — the vital consciousness that makes all three possible.

dp.q: 🔍 The wheel-hub simile across the Upanishads
dp.a: The ratha-nābhi (chariot-wheel hub) simile is one of the most enduring images in Upanishadic philosophy. It appears in: Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.5.15: 'As all spokes are held together in the hub and rim of a wheel, so in this Self (Ātman) all beings, all gods, all worlds, all breaths are held together.' Muṇḍaka 2.2.6: 'In him the channels (nāḍīs) are fixed like spokes in a hub — meditate on the Self as OM.' Praśna 2.6 (this mantra): Prāṇa is the hub; the Vedas, sacrifice, and social order are the spokes. The hub is chosen deliberately over other possible centres (like the axle or the charioteer) because it has a unique property: every spoke meets at the hub. It is the convergence point — the one place where all diversity resolves into unity. This is the core Upanishadic insight: behind the multiplicity of knowledge-systems, rituals, and social structures, there is one sustaining reality.

dp.q: 🔍 Why include kṣatra and brahma?
dp.a: The mention of kṣatra (temporal/warrior power) and brahma (spiritual/priestly power) alongside the three Vedas and sacrifice is significant. In Vedic society, kṣatra and brahma were the two pillars of social order — the rājan (king) and the brāhmaṇa (priest) each depended on the other. By saying both are 'established in Prāṇa', the Upanishad makes a radical claim: neither political power nor spiritual authority is self-grounding. Both depend on the vital force — on life itself. A dead king has no kṣatra; a dead priest has no brahma. This is not a cynical reductionism ('everything is just biology') but an Upanishadic elevation: the life-force (Prāṇa) that sustains king and priest alike is itself a manifestation of Brahman. The message: before you claim authority — whether political or spiritual — recognise that your authority rests on a power you did not create and cannot control.

sk: प्रजापतिश्चरसि गर्भे त्वमेव प्रतिजायसे तुभ्यं प्राण प्रजास्त्विमा बलिं हरन्ति यः प्राणैः प्रतितिष्ठसि ||
ro: prajāpatiḥ · carasi · garbhe · tvam · eva · pratijāyase · tubhyaṁ · prāṇa · prajāḥ · tu · imāḥ · baliṁ · haranti · yaḥ · prāṇaiḥ · pratitiṣṭhasi ||
hi: हे प्राण! तू प्रजापति (सृजनहार) के रूप में गर्भ में विचरण करता है, तू ही (प्रजा के रूप में) पुनः जन्म लेता है। हे प्राण! ये प्रजाएँ तुझे बलि (offerings) चढ़ाती हैं — क्योंकि तू (अन्य) प्राणों (इन्द्रियों) के साथ स्थित रहता है।
en: As Prajāpati (the Lord of creatures) you move in the womb; you yourself are born again (pratijāyase). To you, O Prāṇa, these creatures bring offerings (bali), for you dwell with the (other) vital breaths (prāṇaiḥ).

ws.h: प्रजापति / सृष्टिकर्ता / सब प्राणियों का स्वामी
ws.e: Prajāpati — Lord of creatures / the Creator; Prāṇa is identified with the creative power that enters the womb and generates new life

ws.h: गर्भ में / माता के उदर में
ws.e: in the womb — locative; Prāṇa as Prajāpati enters the womb and becomes the animating force of the embryo

ws.h: पुनः जन्म लेता है / प्रत्येक प्राणी में उत्पन्न होता है
ws.e: you are born again — prati + √jan (to be born); Prāṇa is reborn in every creature; each birth is a re-manifestation of the same cosmic Prāṇa
offering / tribute — the food-offering given to Prāṇa; every act of eating is an offering to the vital breath

ws.h: ले जाते हैं / अर्पित करते हैं
ws.e: they bring / offer — √hṛ (to carry, offer); creatures bring tribute to Prāṇa through the act of eating

gr: prajāpatiḥ carasi garbhe — Prāṇa is now identified with Prajāpati, the Vedic creator-god. The claim is startling: the same breath that sustains your body is the same creative force that animates every embryo in every womb. pratijāyase — 'you are born again': Prāṇa is not born once — it is reborn in every birth. This echoes the Gītā's 'the unborn, eternal Self' that enters body after body. baliṁ haranti — 'they bring offerings': eating is reframed as a sacred act — every meal is a bali (tribute) to Prāṇa. This idea is developed extensively in the prāṇāgnihotra (offering into the fire of the vital breath), a daily Vedic practice. prāṇaiḥ pratitiṣṭhasi — 'you dwell with the vital breaths': even the five sub-prāṇas depend on the one chief Prāṇa.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.7 — The identification of Prāṇa with Prajāpati connects Question 2 back to Question 1, where Prajāpati created the pair of Prāṇa and Rayi. Now Prāṇa itself is Prajāpati — the creator enters its own creation. The concept of eating as 'bali to Prāṇa' is the basis of the prāṇāgnihotra ritual described in Chāndogya 5.19-24 and Manu-smṛti 3.84-86. The Taittirīya Upanishad (3.2-6) similarly elevates food (anna) and Prāṇa to cosmic principles.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्राण को 'प्रजापति' कहना — यह ब्रह्म की सृष्टि-शक्ति (creative power) को दर्शाता है। गर्भ में प्रवेश करना — यह जीव (individual soul) का पुनर्जन्म नहीं, अपितु ब्रह्म की सर्वव्यापकता है जो प्रत्येक नए शरीर में प्रकट होती है।
advaita.en: Shankara says calling Prāṇa 'Prajāpati' reveals Brahman's creative power. Entering the womb is not the rebirth of an individual soul but the manifestation of Brahman's omnipresence in every new body.
advaita.ins: The same breath that fills your lungs right now filled your first cry at birth. And it will fill the first cry of a child born tomorrow. Prāṇa doesn't age, multiply, or die — it re-enters.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण का प्रजापति-रूप ईश्वर की अन्तर्यामित्व (indwelling) शक्ति है। भगवान् गर्भ में जीव के साथ प्रवेश करते हैं — जैसे गीता (18.61) में कहा: 'ईश्वरः सर्वभूतानां हृद्देशे तिष्ठति'।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Prāṇa's Prajāpati-form is the Lord's indwelling (antaryāmitva) power. The Lord enters the womb along with the jīva — as the Gītā (18.61) states: 'The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings.'
vishisht.ins: You were never alone in the womb. The Lord entered with you, as Prāṇa, and has been with you every breath since. Your offerings of food are not charity — they're rent for a tenant who was there before you.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'गर्भे चरसि' — प्राण गर्भ में विचरण करता है — यह सृजनात्मक शक्ति (creative force) का वर्णन है जो प्रत्येक जन्म में नए शरीर का निर्माण करती है। 'बलिं हरन्ति' — भोजन एक यज्ञ है जिसमें प्राण अग्नि है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'garbhe carasi' — Prāṇa moving in the womb — describes the creative force that fashions a new body at every birth. 'Baliṁ haranti' — eating is a sacrifice in which Prāṇa is the fire.
aurobindo.ins: Every embryo is a fresh creation. The same force that formed the first cell is the same force that beats your heart now. And every time you eat, you feed that force — not your stomach.

dp.q: 🔍 What is the prāṇāgnihotra?
dp.a: The prāṇāgnihotra (offering into the fire of the vital breath) is a Vedic practice that transforms the mundane act of eating into a sacred ritual. The principle: every meal is an oblation (āhuti) poured into the fire of Prāṇa. The five morsels of food correspond to the five prāṇas: the first morsel is offered to prāṇa ('prāṇāya svāhā'), the second to vyāna, the third to apāna, the fourth to samāna, the fifth to udāna. This practice is described in Chāndogya 5.19-24 (the pañcāgni-vidyā context) and codified in Manu-smṛti 3.84-86. Its significance: it converts every householder's meal into a Vedic sacrifice — no altar, no priest, no fire needed. The eater is the priest, the food is the offering, and the body's digestive fire (jāṭharāgni) is the sacred fire. This democratises sacrifice: anyone who eats mindfully is performing a yajña.

dp.q: 🔍 How is Prāṇa both creator and creature?
dp.a: The mantra makes a paradoxical claim: Prāṇa is Prajāpati (the creator who moves in the womb) and also the creature that is born again (pratijāyase). This paradox is central to Upanishadic thought: the creator enters its own creation. In Vedāntic terms: Brahman (the Absolute) is both the nimitta-kāraṇa (efficient cause — the potter) and the upādāna-kāraṇa (material cause — the clay). It doesn't create from outside; it becomes the creation. Each birth is not a new Prāṇa being manufactured but the same cosmic Prāṇa re-entering a new form — like the same ocean-water filling a new wave. This dissolves the creator-creature duality: the breath in you is not a gift from God — it is God, operating at the vital level. The Taittirīya Upanishad (2.6) expresses this identically: 'Having created, He entered into it (tat sṛṣṭvā tad evānuprāviśat).'

sk: देवानामसि वह्नितमः पितृणां प्रथमा स्वधा ऋषीणां चरितं सत्यमथर्वाङ्गिरसामसि ||
ro: devānām · asi · vahnitamaḥ · pitṝṇāṁ · prathamā · svadhā · ṛṣīṇāṁ · caritaṁ · satyam · atharva-aṅgirasām · asi ||
hi: तू देवताओं का सर्वोत्तम वहनकर्ता (vahnitama — अग्नि/हव्यवाहक) है, पितरों की प्रथम स्वधा (पितृ-तर्पण की आहुति) है, ऋषियों का सत्य-आचरण (चरित) है, और तू अथर्वाङ्गिरसों (अथर्ववेद के ऋषियों) का (सार) है।
en: You are the foremost carrier (vahnitama) of the gods, the first oblation (svadhā) to the ancestors (pitṛs), the true practice (caritaṁ satyam) of the seers (ṛṣis), and you belong to the Atharvan-Aṅgiras tradition.

ws.e: the foremost carrier — superlative of vahni (fire/carrier); Prāṇa carries offerings to the gods as Agni carries oblations; or: Prāṇa is the supreme fire among all fires

ws.h: पितृ-तर्पण की आहुति / पितरों को दी जाने वाली भेंट
ws.e: svadhā — the ritual offering to the ancestors (pitṛs); the exclamation 'svadhā!' accompanies offerings to the departed; Prāṇa is itself the first such offering
practice / conduct — from √car (to move, practice); the seers' (ṛṣis') practice is identified with Prāṇa — their tapas is sustained by the vital breath

ws.h: अथर्ववेद के ऋषियों का / अथर्वन् और अङ्गिरस् परंपरा का
ws.e: of the Atharvans and Aṅgirases — the two ancient priestly families associated with the Atharva Veda; the Prashna Upanishad belongs to this tradition

gr: devānām vahnitamaḥ — Prāṇa is the supreme vahni (fire/carrier) of the gods. The word vahni has a double meaning: (1) fire (agni), which carries oblations upward to the gods; (2) carrier/bearer. In both senses, Prāṇa is the medium through which offerings reach the divine realm. pitṝṇāṁ prathamā svadhā — 'the first svadhā to the ancestors': svadhā is the exclamation accompanying ancestral offerings. Prāṇa is called the 'first' svadhā because the vital breath must exist before any ritual offering can be made. ṛṣīṇāṁ caritaṁ satyam — 'the true practice of the seers': the ṛṣis' tapas (austerity) and satya (truth) are both sustained by Prāṇa. Without the vital breath, there is no tapas, no truth, no seer. atharva-aṅgirasām — this phrase anchors the Prashna Upanishad in the Atharva Veda tradition. The Atharvans and Aṅgirases were priestly families specialising in healing, protective rites, and esoteric knowledge.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.8 — The hymn now places Prāṇa at the centre of all three ritual domains: (1) deva-yajña — sacrifice to the gods (vahnitama); (2) pitṛ-yajña — offering to the ancestors (svadhā); (3) ṛṣi-practice — the tapas and truth of the sages. The mention of Atharva-Aṅgiras locates the Upanishad within the Atharva Veda tradition — the Prashna, Muṇḍaka, and Māṇḍūkya all belong to this Veda.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्राण तीन लोकों को जोड़ता है: देवलोक (दिव्य), पितृलोक (पूर्वज), और ऋषिलोक (ज्ञान)। यह त्रिविध भूमिका प्राण को ब्रह्म का साक्षात् प्रतीक बनाती है — क्योंकि ब्रह्म ही सब लोकों का आधार है।
advaita.en: Shankara says Prāṇa connects three worlds: the divine (deva-loka), the ancestral (pitṛ-loka), and the seer's world (ṛṣi-loka). This threefold role makes Prāṇa a direct symbol of Brahman — for Brahman alone is the foundation of all worlds.
advaita.ins: Three worlds, three rituals, one breath. You feed the gods with fire, the ancestors with svadhā, and the seers with truth — and all three run on the same fuel: the breath you're taking right now.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण भगवान् का वह माध्यम है जिसके द्वारा देवों, पितरों, और ऋषियों — तीनों को सन्तुष्ट किया जाता है। 'अथर्वाङ्गिरस' — यह दर्शाता है कि यह ज्ञान विशेष रूप से अथर्ववेद की परम्परा में सुरक्षित है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Prāṇa is the Lord's medium through which gods, ancestors, and seers are all satisfied. 'Atharva-Aṅgiras' shows this knowledge is specially preserved in the Atharva Veda tradition.
vishisht.ins: The Lord doesn't accept your offering directly — He receives it through the fire of Prāṇa. Your breath is the Lord's postman, delivering every prayer upward.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण तीन प्रकार की चेतना को पोषित करता है: दैवी (divine), पैतृक (ancestral), और ऋषिक (seer-consciousness)। 'चरितं सत्यम्' — ऋषियों का सत्य-आचरण प्राण से ही चलता है; सत्य जीवन-शक्ति के बिना मात्र शब्द है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says Prāṇa nourishes three modes of consciousness: divine, ancestral, and seer-consciousness. 'Caritaṁ satyam' — the seers' practice of truth is powered by Prāṇa; truth without life-force is just words.
aurobindo.ins: Truth isn't a thought — it's a force. The seers didn't just think true things; they lived truth through the power of breath. Without the vital force behind it, truth has no legs.

dp.q: 🔍 What are the three ritual domains?
dp.a: The mantra identifies Prāṇa with three fundamental Vedic ritual domains: (1) Deva-yajña (sacrifice to the gods): Prāṇa is vahnitama — the supreme fire/carrier. In Vedic ritual, Agni (fire) carries oblations to the gods. Prāṇa is identified with this carrying function — the breath is the internal fire that 'carries' all worship upward. (2) Pitṛ-yajña (offering to the ancestors): Prāṇa is prathamā svadhā — the first offering to the departed. 'Svadhā!' is the exclamation accompanying ancestral rites (cf. 'svāhā!' for divine offerings). Prāṇa is called 'first' because without the breath, no ritual can be performed at all — the living must breathe before they can honour the dead. (3) Ṛṣi-practice: Prāṇa is caritaṁ satyam — the true practice of the seers. The ṛṣis' authority rests not on learning but on tapas (austerity) — sustained effort powered by the vital breath. These three domains together cover the entire Vedic universe: the gods above, the ancestors below, and the sages who mediate between the two.

dp.q: 🔍 Why mention Atharva-Aṅgiras?
dp.a: The phrase atharva-aṅgirasām asi ('you are of the Atharvans and Aṅgirases') serves two purposes: Lineage-marker: the Prashna Upanishad belongs to the Atharva Veda, and this phrase anchors it in its parent tradition. The Atharvans (from ṛṣi Atharvan) and Aṅgirases (from ṛṣi Aṅgiras) were the two founding priestly families of this Veda. Content-marker: the Atharva Veda is the Veda of practical knowledge — healing, protection, and the study of the vital forces (prāṇa-vidyā). By identifying Prāṇa with this tradition, the hymn claims that prāṇa-vidyā is the Atharva Veda's central teaching. This is historically significant: while the Ṛg Veda centres on hymns, the Yajur Veda on sacrifice, and the Sāma Veda on chant, the Atharva Veda's distinctive contribution to Indian thought is its focus on the vital and the embodied — healing, longevity, and the forces that sustain life.

sk: इन्द्रस्त्वं प्राण तेजसा रुद्रो ऽसि परिरक्षिता त्वमन्तरिक्षे चरसि सूर्यस्त्वं ज्योतिषां पतिः ||
ro: indraḥ · tvaṁ · prāṇa · tejasā · rudraḥ · asi · parirakṣitā · tvam · antarikṣe · carasi · sūryaḥ · tvaṁ · jyotiṣāṁ · patiḥ ||
hi: हे प्राण! तू तेज (शौर्य/बल) से इन्द्र है, तू रुद्र (संहारक) है — (सब का) परिरक्षक (रक्षा करने वाला) है। तू अन्तरिक्ष में विचरण करता है। तू सूर्य है — ज्योतियों (प्रकाशों) का पति (स्वामी) है।
en: You are Indra, O Prāṇa, by your splendour (tejas). You are Rudra, the protector. You move in the mid-space (antarikṣa). You are the sun, the lord of all lights (jyotiṣāṁ patiḥ).

ws.e: Indra — king of the gods, lord of power and might; Prāṇa is Indra because it is the mightiest force in the body

ws.h: तेज से / बल से / प्रताप से
ws.e: by splendour / by power — instrumental case of tejas; Prāṇa's Indra-nature manifests through its radiant force
Rudra — the fierce god of storms and destruction; Prāṇa is Rudra because when it departs (death), it destroys the body

ws.h: सब ओर से रक्षा करने वाला
ws.e: protector — pari (around) + √rakṣ (to guard); Prāṇa protects the body from all directions; Rudra destroys enemies but protects devotees
lord of lights — jyotiṣām (of lights, gen. pl.) + pati (lord); the sun is the master of all luminaries; Prāṇa = the cosmic light-source

gr: indraḥ tvaṁ tejasā — Prāṇa is identified with Indra (the king of gods) specifically through tejas (splendour, fiery power). In the body, Prāṇa is the mightiest force — just as Indra is mightiest among gods. rudraḥ asi parirakṣitā — Prāṇa is Rudra, the fierce one (from √rud, to cry/roar). But Rudra is also parirakṣitā (protector) — the same force that destroys (at death) also protects (during life). This dual nature (destroyer-protector) is characteristic of both Rudra and Prāṇa. antarikṣe carasi — 'you move in the mid-space': the antarikṣa (atmospheric space) is Vāyu's (wind's) domain. Prāṇa = Vāyu, the cosmic wind. jyotiṣāṁ patiḥ — 'lord of lights': Prāṇa = Sūrya (sun), the source from which all lesser lights derive.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.9 — The verse identifies Prāṇa with four major Vedic deities across the three cosmic planes: (1) Indra — heaven (dyu-loka); (2) Rudra — the middle region; (3) Vāyu — the atmosphere (antarikṣa); (4) Sūrya — the visible sky. This maps to the trikāṇḍa (three-realm) cosmology of the Vedas. The identification of Prāṇa with Rudra is notable: in later Shaiva philosophy, Rudra/Shiva becomes the supreme deity. Here the Upanishad already seeds that identification by calling Prāṇa both Rudra (destructive aspect) and parirakṣitā (protective aspect).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्राण की इन्द्र, रुद्र, सूर्य आदि से अभिन्नता सगुण ब्रह्म (Brahman with attributes) की उपासना के लिए है। प्रत्येक देवता ब्रह्म का एक पहलू है; प्राण उन सबका अधिष्ठान (substratum) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the identification of Prāṇa with Indra, Rudra, and Sūrya serves saguṇa-upāsanā (meditation on Brahman with attributes). Each deity is an aspect of Brahman; Prāṇa is the substratum of them all.
advaita.ins: Indra, Rudra, Sun — three masks, one face. The Upanishad doesn't ask you to worship three gods. It asks you to see one Prāṇa wearing three costumes: power, destruction-protection, and light.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण ईश्वर की शक्ति, रक्षा, और प्रकाश — तीन विभूतियाँ (glories) प्रकट करता है। इन्द्र = शक्ति, रुद्र = रक्षा, सूर्य = ज्ञान-प्रकाश। ये तीनों भगवान् के गुण हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says Prāṇa manifests three of the Lord's vibhūtis (glories): Indra = power, Rudra = protection, Sūrya = the light of knowledge. These three are attributes of the Lord.
vishisht.ins: Power without protection destroys. Protection without light is blind. Light without power is idle. The Lord combines all three in one breath — and that breath is in you.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — इन्द्र = दिव्य मानसिक शक्ति (divine mental power), रुद्र = परिवर्तनकारी शक्ति (transformative force), सूर्य = सुप्रामेंटल प्रकाश (supramental light)। प्राण इन तीनों स्तरों पर कार्य करता है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees Indra as divine mental power, Rudra as the transformative force (that destroys the old to make way for the new), and Sūrya as supramental light. Prāṇa operates on all three levels.
aurobindo.ins: Indra conquers, Rudra transforms, the Sun illuminates. These aren't just mythological roles — they're stages of consciousness. First you break through (Indra), then you purify (Rudra), then you see (Sun). And all three are powered by one engine: the breath.

dp.q: 🔍 Prāṇa as Rudra: destroyer and protector
dp.a: The identification of Prāṇa with Rudra is especially rich because Rudra embodies a paradox: he is both the destroyer and the protector. The same quality applies to Prāṇa: As destroyer: when Prāṇa departs the body (death), it destroys the entire organism. The faculties, the senses, the mind — all cease. In this role, Prāṇa is the god of death. As protector: while Prāṇa remains in the body, it guards against death. It maintains body temperature, circulates nutrients, fights infection (through immune response), and sustains consciousness. In this role, Prāṇa is the guardian deity. This dual nature is captured in the mantra's juxtaposition: rudraḥ asi parirakṣitā — 'you are Rudra, the protector.' The destroyer is the protector. This is not a contradiction but a recognition that the same force that ends life is the force that sustains it — just as the same fire that warms you can burn you. The Śvetāśvatara Upanishad (3.2-4) develops this Rudra-Prāṇa identification further, eventually identifying Rudra with the supreme Brahman.

dp.q: 🔍 The three cosmic planes in this verse
dp.a: The mantra maps Prāṇa onto the Vedic trikāṇḍa (three-realm cosmology): (1) Dyu-loka (heaven): Prāṇa = Indra (king of the gods) and Sūrya (lord of lights). These are celestial powers. (2) Antarikṣa (mid-space/atmosphere): 'You move in the antarikṣa' — Prāṇa = Vāyu (wind). The atmosphere is the domain of the wind-god. (3) Pṛthivī (earth): implied through Rudra as parirakṣitā (protector of earthly beings). The hymn systematically claims every cosmic level for Prāṇa: it rules in heaven (as Indra/Sun), moves through the atmosphere (as Vāyu), and protects on earth (as Rudra). This total coverage — heaven, atmosphere, earth — means there is no realm where Prāṇa is absent. The same structure appears in the Gāyatrī mantra's three pādas (bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ) and in the Puruṣa Sūkta's description of the Cosmic Person spanning all three worlds.

sk: यदा त्वमभिवर्षस्यथेमाः प्राण ते प्रजाः आनन्दरूपास्तिष्ठन्ति कामायान्नं भविष्यतीति ||
ro: yadā · tvam · abhivarṣasi · atha · imāḥ · prāṇa · te · prajāḥ · ānanda-rūpāḥ · tiṣṭhanti · kāmāya · annaṁ · bhaviṣyati · iti ||
hi: हे प्राण! जब तू (पर्जन्य/वर्षा-रूप में) वर्षा करता है, तब तेरी ये प्रजाएँ (सब प्राणी) आनन्दरूपा (आनन्द से भरी) हो जाती हैं — (यह सोचकर कि) 'इच्छानुसार अन्न (भोजन) प्राप्त होगा।'
en: When you pour rain (abhivarṣasi), O Prāṇa, then these creatures of yours become filled with joy (ānanda-rūpāḥ), thinking: 'Food will come according to our desire (kāma).'

ws.e: you rain / you pour down — abhi + √vṛṣ (to rain); Prāṇa as Parjanya (rain-god) showers rain upon the earth
filled with joy / having the form of bliss — ānanda (bliss) + rūpa (form); creatures literally become 'joy-shaped' when rain comes

ws.h: इच्छा के अनुसार / कामना-पूर्ति के लिए
ws.e: for desire / according to wish — dative of kāma; the rain fulfils the creatures' desire for food
food — from √ad (to eat); anna is the foundation of the food-chain; rain produces grain, grain feeds creatures

gr: abhivarṣasi — 'you rain': this directly connects to Question 1 where Prāṇa was identified with the sun and Rayi with the moon/matter. Here the cycle completes: Prāṇa (as sun) draws up water, then (as Parjanya) pours it down as rain. ānanda-rūpāḥ — 'filled with joy': the compound is striking — creatures don't just feel joy, they become joy (rūpa = form/essence). Rain transforms the emotional state of all living beings. kāmāya annaṁ bhaviṣyati — 'food will come as desired': the thought inside creatures' minds. This is the Vedic understanding of happiness: it rests on the assurance of food. Anna (food) is the base of the Taittirīya hierarchy: anna → prāṇa → manas → vijñāna → ānanda.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.10 — The rain-food-joy chain echoes the Taittirīya Upanishad's famous statement: 'From food, creatures are born; by food, once born, they grow' (Tai. 2.2). The Chāndogya (7.10) similarly states that anna (food) is greater than āpaḥ (water), establishing the hierarchy: rain → food → life → joy. The word ānanda-rūpa ('joy-formed') anticipates the Taittirīya's ānandamaya kośa — the sheath of bliss as the innermost layer of being.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — वर्षा से आनन्द — यह दर्शाता है कि ब्रह्म (प्राण-रूप में) सब प्राणियों के सुख का कारण है। 'आनन्दरूपाः' — जीव का स्वाभाविक स्वरूप ही आनन्द है; वर्षा (अन्न की आशा) उस आनन्द को जगाती है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the joy from rain shows that Brahman (as Prāṇa) is the cause of all creatures' happiness. 'Ānanda-rūpāḥ' — the natural state of the jīva is bliss; rain (the hope of food) awakens that inherent bliss.
advaita.ins: Rain doesn't create joy — it uncovers it. The joy was always there, buried under the anxiety of hunger. When rain falls, anxiety lifts, and what remains is your natural state: bliss.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — भगवान् वर्षा के माध्यम से सब प्राणियों का पालन करते हैं। गीता (3.14): 'अन्नाद्भवन्ति भूतानि पर्जन्यादन्नसम्भवः' — अन्न से प्राणी उत्पन्न होते हैं, पर्जन्य (वर्षा) से अन्न उत्पन्न होता है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says the Lord nourishes all creatures through rain. As the Gītā (3.14) states: 'From food beings are born; from rain food is produced.' This rain-food-life chain is the Lord's sustaining mechanism.
vishisht.ins: The Lord doesn't feed you directly — He sends rain, rain grows grain, grain feeds you. This chain of care is how divine love works: not by miracle, but by system.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — वर्षा चेतना की कृपा (grace) का प्रतीक है — जब दिव्य शक्ति (प्राण) नीचे बरसती है, तो जीवन में आनन्द स्वतः प्रकट होता है। 'आनन्दरूपाः' — जीव आनन्द-स्वरूप बन जाते हैं, न कि बाहर से आनन्द पाते हैं।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo sees rain as a symbol of the grace of consciousness — when the divine force (Prāṇa) descends, joy manifests spontaneously in life. 'Ānanda-rūpāḥ' — creatures become bliss-formed, not merely happy from external causes.
aurobindo.ins: When grace rains down, you don't 'get' joy — you become it. The Upanishad's word is precise: ānanda-rūpa, 'joy-formed'. You don't possess happiness; you become happiness.

dp.q: 🔍 The rain-food-joy chain in Vedic thought
dp.a: The Vedic tradition identifies a cosmic cycle linking rain, food, and joy: Sun (Prāṇa) evaporates water → Rain (Parjanya) falls → Food (anna) grows → Creatures (prajā) eat → Joy (ānanda) arises. This chain is codified across the Upanishads: Taittirīya 2.2: 'From food, creatures are born; by food, once born, they grow; food is eaten by beings and in turn eats them.' Chāndogya 7.10: 'Food is greater than water' — in the ascending meditation on the Infinite. Bhagavad Gītā 3.14-15: 'From food beings are born; from rain food is produced; from sacrifice rain arises; sacrifice springs from action (karma).' The Upanishadic insight is that joy is not an accident but the natural result of a cosmic chain that begins with Prāṇa (the sun) and ends with ānanda (bliss). When any link breaks — drought, famine, disease — joy vanishes. The sages concluded: maintain the chain through sacrifice and right living, and joy is assured.

dp.q: 🔍 What does ānanda-rūpa mean?
dp.a: The compound ānanda-rūpa (आनन्दरूप) literally means 'having bliss as one's form' or 'bliss-shaped'. This is stronger than saying creatures 'feel' joy — it says they become joy. The distinction matters in Vedāntic philosophy: External joy (viṣayānanda) comes from outside and is temporary — you feel happy when you get what you want, but the happiness fades. Intrinsic joy (svarūpānanda) is your natural state — it doesn't come from outside but is uncovered when external anxiety is removed. The Taittirīya Upanishad (2.5) describes ānandamaya kośa (the bliss-sheath) as the innermost layer of the self — deeper than body, breath, mind, and intellect. When rain falls and creatures become ānanda-rūpa, the Upanishad suggests that the removal of food-anxiety doesn't create joy but reveals the bliss that was always the core of their being. This is the Upanishadic theory of happiness: you are not a body that sometimes feels happy; you are bliss (ānanda) that sometimes feels afraid.

sk: व्रात्यस्त्वं प्राणैकर्षिरत्ता विश्वस्य सत्पतिः वयमाद्यस्य दातारः पिता त्वं मातरिश्वन् ||
ro: vrātyaḥ · tvaṁ · prāṇa · eka-ṛṣiḥ · attā · viśvasya · sat-patiḥ · vayam · ādyasya · dātāraḥ · pitā · tvaṁ · mātariśvan ||
hi: हे प्राण! तू व्रात्य (दीक्षा-रहित, स्वतंत्र, अव्रती) है, तू एकर्षि (एकमात्र ऋषि / एकमात्र द्रष्टा) है, तू सब का भक्षक (अत्ता) है, तू विश्व का सत्पति (सच्चा स्वामी) है। हम (अन्य देव) तुझे भोज्य पदार्थ (आद्य) देने वाले हैं। हे मातरिश्वन् (वायु)! तू (सबका) पिता है।
en: You are the Vrātya (the unconsecrated wanderer), O Prāṇa, the sole seer (eka-ṛṣi), the devourer (attā) of all, the true lord (sat-pati) of the universe. We are the givers of what is to be eaten (ādya). O Mātariśvan (Wind)! You are the father.

ws.h: व्रात्य — संस्कार-रहित / दीक्षा-रहित / स्वतंत्र विचरण करने वाला
ws.e: Vrātya — one who is outside the Vedic initiation system; a wanderer who follows no convention; the Atharva Veda (book 15) has the famous Vrātya Sūkta identifying the Supreme Being as a Vrātya
the sole seer — eka (one) + ṛṣi (seer); Prāṇa is the one true seer, because without the vital breath no vision (inner or outer) is possible
the devourer / eater — from √ad (to eat); Prāṇa consumes everything at death; all beings are its food
lord of the existent / true lord — sat (being/truth) + pati (lord); Prāṇa is the master of all that exists

ws.h: वायु / वायुदेव (जो माता/अन्तरिक्ष में श्वसन करता है)
ws.e: Mātariśvan — a Vedic name for Wind (Vāyu); etymologically: 'who breathes (śvas) in the mother (mātari)' — the wind that moves in the atmosphere (the cosmic mother)

gr: vrātyaḥ — this is the most surprising epithet. A Vrātya was a person outside the Vedic ritual system — uninitiated, convention-free. The Atharva Veda (book 15, Vrātya-kāṇḍa) identifies the supreme Vrātya with Prajāpati and ultimately with the Absolute. Calling Prāṇa a Vrātya means: Prāṇa is beyond all ritual categories; it cannot be contained by any system. eka-ṛṣiḥ — 'the sole seer': all other seers (ṛṣis) see through the power of Prāṇa; Prāṇa alone sees independently. attā viśvasya — 'devourer of all': at death, Prāṇa 'eats' the body and all its faculties. This echoes Kaṭha 1.2.25: 'Brahman is the food of death; who knows that death is the condiment?' mātariśvan — an ancient Vedic name for Vāyu (Wind), etymologically 'who breathes in the mother (atmosphere)'. By calling Prāṇa 'father' and 'Mātariśvan', the hymn makes Prāṇa the parent of all creatures.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.11 — The Vrātya identification is remarkable and ties the Prashna directly to Atharva Veda 15 (Vrātya-kāṇḍa), where the Vrātya is progressively identified with Prajāpati, with the Year, with the cosmic directions, and finally with the supreme Brahman. The term eka-ṛṣi ('sole seer') connects to the Nāsadīya concept of the one who 'saw' before creation. The epithet attā ('devourer') parallels Taittirīya 3.2: 'I am the eater of food; I eat the eater of food.' Mātariśvan appears in RV 1.93.6 and 3.29.11 as the being who brought fire from heaven — another aspect of Prāṇa's role as the cosmic intermediary.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'व्रात्य' — प्राण (= ब्रह्म) किसी भी संस्कार या दीक्षा से बाँधा नहीं जा सकता; यह नित्य-मुक्त है। 'अत्ता' — प्रलय-काल में सब कुछ प्राण (ब्रह्म) में विलीन हो जाता है — यही 'भक्षण' है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'Vrātya' means Prāṇa (= Brahman) cannot be bound by any sacrament or initiation; it is eternally free. 'Attā' — at the time of cosmic dissolution, everything dissolves into Prāṇa (Brahman) — this is the 'devouring'.
advaita.ins: You can't initiate Brahman. You can't put it through a ceremony. It was there before the first ritual was invented, and it will be there after the last one is forgotten. That's what Vrātya means: beyond all categories, including sacred ones.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'व्रात्य' — भगवान् किसी नियम से बँधे नहीं; वे स्वेच्छा से विचरण करते हैं। 'सत्पतिः' — सत् (समस्त अस्तित्व) के स्वामी — यह भगवान् की सार्वभौमिकता (sovereignty) है। 'पिता' — भगवान् सबके जनक हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'Vrātya' means the Lord is bound by no rule; He wanders freely. 'Sat-pati' — lord of all existence — declares the Lord's sovereignty. 'Pitā' — the Lord is the father of all.
vishisht.ins: God is not a citizen of any country, a member of any caste, or a follower of any rule. He's the Vrātya — the divine wanderer. And yet He's also the father. Free but responsible. Unbound but caring.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'व्रात्य' — प्राण सब सामाजिक और धार्मिक वर्गीकरण (classification) से परे है। 'एकर्षि' — एकमात्र द्रष्टा — यह चेतना का वह स्तर है जो सब देखता है किन्तु किसी से नहीं दिखता। 'अत्ता' — यह चेतना सब अनुभवों को ग्रहण (absorb) करती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'Vrātya' means Prāṇa is beyond all social and religious classification. 'Eka-ṛṣi' — the sole seer — is the level of consciousness that sees everything but is seen by nothing. 'Attā' — this consciousness absorbs all experiences.
aurobindo.ins: The sole seer. The one who was watching before the first pair of eyes opened. It doesn't need your rituals to exist, and it doesn't need your categories to function. It's the Vrātya — the free one.

dp.q: 🔍 Who is the Vrātya?
dp.a: The Vrātya (व्रात्य) is one of the most enigmatic figures in Vedic literature. In social terms, a vrātya was an outsider — a person who had not undergone Vedic initiation (upanayana) and therefore stood outside the varṇa system. Vrātyas were wandering ascetics, warriors, or ecstatics who followed their own path. The Atharva Veda book 15 (Vrātya-kāṇḍa) transforms this social outsider into a cosmic principle: 'The Vrātya stood; He performed tapas; He created Prajāpati... He encompasses the worlds... He is this all.' The Vrātya becomes the supreme Being who existed before creation, before ritual, before the Vedas themselves. By calling Prāṇa 'Vrātya', the Prashna Upanishad makes a profound statement: the vital force that sustains your body is the same trans-conventional, pre-ritual, category-defying reality that the Atharva Veda hymns celebrate. Prāṇa is not bound by the Vedic system — it is prior to the system. Without Prāṇa, there would be no Vedas, no rituals, no initiations. The breath was there before the first hymn was composed.

dp.q: 🔍 What does 'devourer of all' (attā viśvasya) mean?
dp.a: The epithet attā viśvasya ('eater/devourer of all') has multiple layers: (1) Death: at the moment of death, Prāṇa 'devours' the body — all faculties collapse into it and are absorbed. The Kaṭha Upanishad (1.2.25) says: 'For this great Brahman, death is the condiment.' Everything ends up as food for the vital force. (2) Cosmic dissolution (pralaya): at the end of a cosmic cycle, all beings dissolve back into the primal force — Prāṇa 'eats' the entire universe. (3) Metabolic process: Prāṇa literally 'eats' food — digestion is the process by which the vital breath converts food into energy. The Taittirīya (3.2) celebrates this: 'I am the eater of food! I eat the eater of food! I have overcome the whole world!' (4) Experiential absorption: every experience — sight, sound, thought — is 'consumed' by consciousness through Prāṇa. Without the vital breath, no experience can be processed. The 'devourer' is not destructive but transformative: it converts the raw material of the world (food, experience, matter) into life, consciousness, and eventually spirit.

sk: या ते तनूर्वाचि प्रतिष्ठिता या श्रोत्रे या च चक्षुषि या च मनसि संतता शिवां तां कुरु मोत्क्रामीः ||
ro: yā · te · tanūḥ · vāci · pratiṣṭhitā · yā · śrotre · yā · ca · cakṣuṣi · yā · ca · manasi · santatā · śivāṁ · tāṁ · kuru · mā · utkrāmīḥ ||
hi: हे प्राण! तेरी जो तनु (रूप/शक्ति) वाणी में प्रतिष्ठित है, जो श्रोत्र (कान) में है, जो चक्षु (नेत्र) में है, और जो मन में सन्तत (व्याप्त/फैली) है — उस (तनु) को शिव (शुभ/मंगलकारी) बना (रख)। (शरीर से) मत जा! (उत्क्रमण मत कर!)
en: That form (tanū) of yours which is established in speech, which is in hearing, which is in sight, and which pervades (santatā) the mind — make it auspicious (śiva)! Do not depart (mā utkrāmīḥ)!

ws.e: form / body / self-manifestation — tanū here means the specific 'form' or 'aspect' of Prāṇa present in each faculty
pervading / extended — sam + √tan (to stretch); Prāṇa's form is stretched/woven through all the faculties like a thread through beads
auspicious / benevolent — śiva (auspicious); the gods pray that Prāṇa's form remain kind and life-sustaining

ws.h: मत जा / (शरीर से) उत्क्रमण मत कर
ws.e: do not depart! — mā (prohibitive particle) + utkrāmīḥ (2nd person aorist injunctive of ut + √kram); a plea: stay in the body, do not leave

gr: yā te tanūḥ vāci...śrotre...cakṣuṣi...manasi — Prāṇa has a 'tanū' (form/aspect) in each faculty: speech, hearing, sight, and mind. These four are the gateways of conscious experience. santatā — 'pervading/stretched through': Prāṇa's form is not localised in one faculty but runs through all of them like a continuous thread. śivāṁ tāṁ kuru — 'make it auspicious': a prayer-formula. The gods, having recognised Prāṇa's supremacy, now request that its presence remain benign. This is significant: a force that can sustain can also destroy (cf. mantra 9: 'rudraḥ asi'). The gods ask for the śiva (gentle/auspicious) aspect, not the rudra (fierce) aspect. mā utkrāmīḥ — 'do not depart!': the most poignant line in the hymn. Having seen what happens when Prāṇa begins to leave (mantra 4), the gods plead: stay. This is, at its core, a prayer against death.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.12 — The plea 'mā utkrāmīḥ' (do not depart) echoes several Vedic prayers for longevity and life. Compare Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.3.28: 'Lead me from death to immortality' (mṛtyor mā amṛtaṁ gamaya). The word śiva here is pre-Shaiva — it means 'auspicious/benevolent' without yet referring to the deity Shiva. The four faculties named (vāk, śrotra, cakṣuḥ, manas) are the same four from mantra 2, now addressed as vessels of Prāṇa's form.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'शिवां तां कुरु' — यह प्रार्थना है कि प्राण शुभ (auspicious) बना रहे, अर्थात् शरीर में स्थित रहे और जीवन-दायक बना रहे। 'मोत्क्रामीः' — मृत्यु न हो — यह जीवन की प्रार्थना है। किन्तु अन्ततः प्राण (ब्रह्म) कभी 'जाता' नहीं — केवल उपाधि (body-limitation) गिरती है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'śivāṁ tāṁ kuru' is a prayer that Prāṇa remain auspicious — stay in the body and sustain life. 'Mā utkrāmīḥ' — let death not come — is the prayer of life itself. But ultimately Prāṇa (Brahman) never 'departs' — only the body-limitation (upādhi) falls away.
advaita.ins: The deepest prayer is the simplest: don't leave. Every breath you take is that prayer being answered. And when it's finally not answered — that's not Prāṇa leaving. That's the container breaking. The breath was never yours to keep.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'मोत्क्रामीः' — यह भक्त की विनती है: 'हे भगवान्, मुझे न छोड़ो!' प्राण ईश्वर का आन्तरिक रूप है; उसका बने रहना — ईश्वर की कृपा (grace) है।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'mā utkrāmīḥ' is the devotee's plea: 'O Lord, do not abandon me!' Prāṇa is the Lord's inner form; its remaining is the Lord's grace.
vishisht.ins: Every heartbeat is grace. Not a right, not a guarantee — grace. The gods know this, which is why they pray: stay. Stay one more beat.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'शिवाम्' — यह चेतना के शुभ, कल्याणकारी पहलू की प्रार्थना है। प्राण में विनाशक (rudra) और कल्याणकारी (śiva) दोनों शक्तियाँ हैं; साधक शिव-पक्ष की प्रार्थना करता है। 'मोत्क्रामीः' — शरीर को तब तक सुरक्षित रखो जब तक आध्यात्मिक कार्य पूरा न हो जाए।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'śivām' is a prayer for the auspicious, benevolent aspect of consciousness. Prāṇa contains both destructive (rudra) and auspicious (śiva) potencies; the seeker prays for the śiva aspect. 'Mā utkrāmīḥ' — keep the body safe until the spiritual work is complete.
aurobindo.ins: The body is a workshop, not a prison. You need it intact long enough to finish the work. That's the prayer: not 'let me live forever' but 'let me live long enough to see.'

dp.q: 🔍 Why 'make it śiva' (auspicious)?
