dp.a: The prayer śivāṁ tāṁ kuru ('make that form auspicious') acknowledges something crucial: Prāṇa has both benign and terrible aspects. In mantra 9, Prāṇa was called Rudra — the fierce, destructive aspect. In this mantra, the gods ask for the śiva aspect — the gentle, life-sustaining form. The word śiva here is pre-Shaiva — it simply means 'auspicious, kindly, benevolent' (as opposed to rudra/ugra = fierce). The prayer recognises that the same force that keeps you alive is the force that will kill you: Prāṇa sustains the body moment by moment, but when it departs, death is instantaneous. The gods' prayer is: let the force remain in its sustaining mode, not its destroying mode. In later Hindu theology, this duality becomes the Rudra-Śiva polarity — the same god who destroys the universe (Rudra) is also the most compassionate protector (Śiva). The Prashna's usage shows this polarity already present at the Upanishadic level.

dp.q: 🔍 'Do not depart!' — the universal prayer against death
dp.a: The plea mā utkrāmīḥ ('do not depart!') is one of the most emotionally resonant lines in the Upanishads. It distils the human condition into three words: we want to live. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.3.28) expresses the same yearning: mṛtyor mā amṛtaṁ gamaya — 'Lead me from death to immortality.' The Vedic tradition does not deny or suppress the fear of death; it addresses it head-on. The departure-test (mantra 4) showed what death looks like — all faculties collapsing when Prāṇa leaves. Now, having seen that preview, the faculties pray: don't let it happen. At the deepest level, however, the Upanishads answer this prayer not by granting biological immortality but by revealing that the true Self (Ātman) never departs. As Shankara notes: Prāṇa (= Brahman) never actually 'leaves' — what falls away is the body (upādhi). The prayer 'do not depart' is ultimately fulfilled not by Prāṇa staying in the body forever, but by the seeker realising that he is Prāṇa — and Prāṇa, being Brahman, can never die.

sk: प्राणस्येदं वशे सर्वं त्रिदिवे यत्प्रतिष्ठितम् मातेव पुत्रान्रक्षस्व श्रीश्च प्रज्ञां च विधेहि न इति ||
ro: prāṇasya · idaṁ · vaśe · sarvaṁ · tridive · yat · pratiṣṭhitam · mātā · iva · putrān · rakṣasva · śrīḥ · ca · prajñāṁ · ca · vidhehi · naḥ · iti ||
hi: प्राण के वश (अधीन) में यह सब कुछ है — जो त्रिदिव (तीनों लोकों) में प्रतिष्ठित है। जैसे माता पुत्रों की रक्षा करती है, वैसे (हमारी) रक्षा कर। और हमें श्री (समृद्धि) तथा प्रज्ञा (ज्ञान) — दोनों प्रदान कर। — इति (इस प्रकार स्तुति समाप्त हुई)।
en: All this is in the power (vaśa) of Prāṇa — whatever is established in the three heavens (tridiva). Protect us as a mother (mātā) protects her children (putrān). Grant us prosperity (śrī) and wisdom (prajñā). — Thus (ends the hymn of praise).

ws.e: in the power of / under the control of — locative of vaśa (power, will); everything is subject to Prāṇa's authority
in the three heavens / in the triple world — tri (three) + diva (heaven); can mean 'heaven' specifically or 'the three worlds' (earth, atmosphere, heaven)

ws.h: माता की तरह / माँ के समान
ws.e: like a mother — the tenderest of Vedic similes; Prāṇa is asked to protect with maternal care
prosperity / splendour / wealth — the outer fullness; paired with prajñā (inner wisdom)
wisdom / discernment — pra + √jñā (to know); the inner fullness; the highest faculty of the mind

gr: prāṇasya vaśe sarvam — 'everything is in Prāṇa's power': the culminating declaration. After the hymn has identified Prāṇa with every cosmic force, this sentence sums up: nothing escapes its sovereignty. mātā iva putrān rakṣasva — 'protect us as a mother protects her children': the maternal simile is deliberately chosen over the paternal (though mantra 11 called Prāṇa 'pitā'). The mother-protection is unconditional — a mother does not protect her children based on merit or conduct. This is the Upanishadic understanding of grace: Prāṇa sustains all creatures without discrimination. śrīś ca prajñāṁ ca — the twin boons: śrī (material prosperity) and prajñā (spiritual wisdom). The Upanishad does not ask for one at the expense of the other; it asks for both — the complete human life: successful in the world (śrī) and awake within (prajñā). iti — 'thus': marks the end of the hymn of praise (mantras 5-13).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: prashna_upanishad_2.13 — The concluding verse of the hymn contains the celebrated prayer 'mātā iva putrān rakṣasva' — one of the most tender lines in the Upanishads. The dual request for śrī and prajñā echoes the Isha Upanishad's integration of vidyā and avidyā (knowledge and works). The Taittirīya's convocation address (1.11) similarly asks for both: 'May śrī come to me, may wisdom come to me.' The hymn's structure (mantras 5-13) follows a classic Vedic pattern: identification → praise → prayer.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'श्री' और 'प्रज्ञा' — दोनों की प्रार्थना — यह दर्शाता है कि ज्ञान-मार्ग और लोक-मार्ग दोनों प्राण (ब्रह्म) पर निर्भर हैं। 'मातेव' — माता की उपमा — ब्रह्म की निर्हेतुक कृपा (unconditional grace) का प्रतीक है।
advaita.en: Shankara says the prayer for both 'śrī' and 'prajñā' shows that both the worldly path and the knowledge-path depend on Prāṇa (Brahman). 'Mātā iva' — the mother-simile symbolises Brahman's unconditional grace.
advaita.ins: The Upanishad doesn't make you choose between wealth and wisdom. It asks for both — because both flow from the same source. A mother doesn't say 'I'll protect your body or your mind, pick one.' She protects all of you.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'मातेव रक्षस्व' — भगवान् की वात्सल्य-भक्ति (motherly love) यहाँ प्रकट है। भगवान् माता की तरह बिना शर्त रक्षा करते हैं। 'श्री और प्रज्ञा' — ये भगवान् की दो शक्तियाँ हैं: श्री (लक्ष्मी) और प्रज्ञा (ज्ञान-शक्ति)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'mātā iva rakṣasva' reveals the Lord's vātsalya-bhakti (motherly love). The Lord protects unconditionally, like a mother. 'Śrī and prajñā' are two of the Lord's powers: Śrī (Lakṣmī/prosperity) and prajñā (the power of knowledge).
vishisht.ins: A mother's love asks nothing in return. That's the model for divine grace. The Lord doesn't protect you because you earned it — He protects you because you're His.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'श्री' = बाह्य पूर्णता (outer fullness), 'प्रज्ञा' = आन्तरिक प्रकाश (inner light)। दोनों एक ही चेतना (प्राण) से प्राप्त होते हैं। सच्ची आध्यात्मिकता भौतिक जीवन को नकारती नहीं, अपितु उसे रूपान्तरित (transform) करती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'śrī' = outer fullness, 'prajñā' = inner light. Both come from the same consciousness (Prāṇa). True spirituality does not reject material life but transforms it.
aurobindo.ins: Don't choose between the inner and the outer. The mother doesn't split her children into 'spiritual' and 'worldly'. She feeds, clothes, educates — the whole child. Ask for the whole: prosperity and insight. The source of both is the same breath.

dp.q: 🔍 Why ask for both śrī and prajñā?
dp.a: The dual prayer for śrī (prosperity) and prajñā (wisdom) is a hallmark of the Upanishadic worldview, which rejects the false choice between material success and spiritual illumination. Śrī encompasses material well-being: health, wealth, social standing, and the ability to perform one's duties (dharma). Without śrī, the body cannot be sustained, and the seeker cannot practice. Prajñā encompasses spiritual discernment: the ability to distinguish the real from the unreal, the Self from the not-Self. Without prajñā, śrī becomes bondage. The Isha Upanishad (mantras 9-11) makes the same point: 'Into blind darkness enter those who worship avidyā (works/ignorance); into still greater darkness those who worship vidyā (knowledge) alone. He who knows both together crosses death through avidyā and attains immortality through vidyā.' The message is clear: you need both. A life of wisdom without material capacity is ineffective; a life of material success without wisdom is purposeless. The complete human life integrates śrī (the capacity to act in the world) with prajñā (the light to see where you're going).

dp.q: 🔍 The mother simile in Vedic literature
dp.a: The simile mātā iva putrān rakṣasva ('protect us as a mother protects her children') is one of the most emotionally powerful images in the Upanishads. While the Vedas frequently use paternal imagery for the divine (Dyaus Pitā = Father Sky; Prajāpati = Lord of Creatures), the maternal image carries a different force: (1) Unconditional protection: a father's protection may be conditional on conduct or obedience; a mother's protection is absolute. She protects the weak child even more than the strong one. (2) Intimate, embodied care: the mother doesn't protect from a distance — she holds, feeds, and shelters with her own body. Similarly, Prāṇa doesn't protect the faculties from afar; it pervades them (santatā, mantra 12). (3) Non-judgmental: the mother doesn't ask whether the child 'deserves' protection. This models the Upanishadic understanding of grace: Prāṇa sustains the body without regard to the body's merit. The Śvetāśvatara (4.3) and the Gītā (9.17) similarly use parental imagery: 'I am the father, the mother, the sustainer.' But the Prashna's 'mātā iva' remains unique in its directness and tenderness.
